lessons.title: What is Honey? Composition and Properties
lessons.body: Honey is a thick, sweet liquid made by bees from flower nectar. In Africa, honey comes from many plants like acacia, baobab, eucalyptus, and wildflowers. Its main sugars are glucose and fructose, making up about 80% of its weight. The rest is water (usually 15â20%), plus small amounts of minerals, vitamins, enzymes, and antioxidants. This mix gives honey its energy boost and long shelf life. For example, 1 kilogram of honey contains roughly 3,040 calories. Because it is acidic (pH around 3.9) and low in water, bacteria cannot grow in it. That is why pure honey never spoils if kept sealed. When you harvest, the moisture content matters. In Africa, aim for below 20% moisture. You can check with a simple refractometer, a tool costing about $50. If honey has more water, it will ferment and taste like alcohol. Honey also crystallizes over time. This is normal and does not mean it is fake. To turn it back to liquid, place the jar in warm water (not above 40Â°C). Heating above 60Â°C destroys enzymes and darkens the honey. Different flowers give different colours and flavours. Acacia honey is light and mild; forest honey is dark and strong. For small-scale farmers, understanding these properties helps you decide when to harvest, how to store, and what price to ask. Always store honey in food-grade plastic or glass containers, away from sunlight. Never use metal containers because honey's acid reacts with metal, causing rust and bad taste. Keep your honey in a cool, dry place. With proper handling, your honey can last for years and fetch a good price at local markets or cooperatives.

lessons.title: Types of Bees in Africa: Apis mellifera and Stingless Bees
lessons.body: Africa has two main groups of honey-making bees: Apis mellifera (stinging honeybees) and stingless bees (Meliponula and others). Apis mellifera is the most common. In Africa, there are several subspecies: A. m. scutellata (East and Southern Africa), A. m. adansonii (West and Central Africa), A. m. monticola (mountain regions), and A. m. capensis (South Africa). These bees are aggressive but produce large amounts of honey. A strong colony can give 20â30 kg per year in good conditions. They live in cavitiesâhollow trees, rock crevices, or man-made hives. Stingless bees are smaller, harmless, and produce less honeyâtypically 1â5 kg per year. But their honey is highly valued for medicinal use, often selling for 3â5 times the price of normal honey. They nest in tree trunks, walls, or ground cavities. In Africa, common stingless bee species include Meliponula bocandei and Dactylurina staudingeri. They are found mostly in forests and savannahs. Beekeeping with stingless bees is growing in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. You can keep them in special boxes called meliponaries. Because they do not sting, they are safe near homes and for women and children. However, they need more careful management: they are sensitive to disturbance and need small entrance holes. For a small-scale farmer, Apis mellifera gives more honey but requires protective gear and smoke. Stingless bees give less honey but higher prices and easier handling. Many farmers keep both. To attract wild bees, you can hang a baited hiveâuse beeswax or lemon grass oil as attractant. In Africa, beekeeping with Apis mellifera is more common because of higher yields. But stingless bees are a good option for beginners or those with limited space. Choose based on your market, climate, and comfort with stinging insects.

lessons.title: Beekeeping Equipment for Small-Scale Farmers
lessons.body: To start beekeeping in Africa, you need basic equipment. The most important is a hive. The two common types are the Langstroth hive and the Kenya Top Bar Hive (KTBH). The Langstroth uses frames and is good for high honey yieldsâup to 30 kg per year. It costs about $50â$80. The KTBH is cheaper ($20â$40) and easier to build locally with timber. It uses top bars instead of frames. Both work well, but KTBH is more suitable for African small-scale farmers because it is low-cost and uses local materials. You also need a bee suit. A full suit with veil and gloves protects you from stings. Expect to pay $30â$50. Alternatively, you can wear thick clothing (e.g., overalls) and a hat with a mesh veil. Smoke is your best tool. A bee smoker costs $15â$25. You burn dry grass, cow dung, or cardboard. Smoke calms bees by masking alarm pheromones. A hive tool (a small crowbar) helps pry open hives and lift frames. It costs $5â$10. You also need a bee brush to gently remove bees from combsâ$3â$5. For harvesting, use a honey extractor (manual or electric). A manual extractor costs $80â$150. If you cannot afford one, you can crush and strain combs through a cloth, but this destroys the comb and gives lower quality. Buckets, jars, and a refractometer (for moisture) are also useful. A refractometer costs about $50. For stingless bees, you need smaller boxes with small entrance holes and a syringe or pipette to harvest honey without destroying the nest. Always keep equipment clean. Wash suits and tools after each use. Store hives in a dry, shaded place. In Africa, you can buy equipment from local beekeeping associations or agricultural supply shops. Many NGOs and government programs offer training and subsidized gear. Start smallâtwo or three hivesâand expand as you learn. Proper equipment means fewer stings, healthier bees, and more honey.

lessons.title: Harvesting Honey: Timing and Methods
lessons.body: Harvesting at the right time is critical. In Africa, honey flow depends on rainfall and flowering. In most regions, harvest after the rainy season when flowers are abundant. For example, in East Africa, harvest from June to September and December to February. In West Africa, harvest from October to December. Never harvest when bees are hungry or during droughtâthey need honey to survive. Check the hive: combs should be at least 80% capped (sealed with white wax). If less, wait. Use a smoker to calm bees. Wear your suit. Open the hive gently. Remove one frame or top bar at a time. For Langstroth, use a bee brush to remove bees. For KTBH, lift the bar and brush bees off. Never harvest brood combs (where baby bees grow). Only take honey combs. Leave at least 30% of honey for the colony, especially before a dry season. If you take all, the bees will abscond (leave). For extraction, use a honey extractor for Langstroth frames. Spin the frames to remove honey without breaking comb. For KTBH, you can crush and strain. Cut comb into pieces, mash with a clean potato masher, and strain through a double layer of cheesecloth or nylon mesh into a bucket. Let it sit for 24 hours so wax and debris float. Then pour into clean, dry jars. For stingless bees, harvest with a syringe by sucking honey from potsâdo not destroy the nest. Always harvest in the evening or early morning when bees are calm. Avoid harvesting in the heat of the day. After harvest, return the hive to its stand. Clean up spilled honey to prevent robbing by other bees. Store honey in airtight containers. In Africa, many farmers lose honey due to poor timing. Harvest too early and honey ferments; too late and bees swarm or abscond. With practice, you will learn your local flowering calendar. Record harvest dates and yields each year to improve.

lessons.title: Identifying Quality Honey vs. Adulterated Honey
lessons.body: Adulterated honey is a big problem in African markets. It is honey mixed with sugar syrup, corn syrup, or water. To protect your customers and your reputation, learn to spot fake honey. First, check the label. Pure honey should list only 'honey' as an ingredient. If it says 'honey blend' or 'honey syrup', it is not pure. But many local sellers do not label. So you need simple tests. The water test: put a drop of honey in a glass of water. Pure honey sinks and stays as a lump. Adulterated honey dissolves quickly. The thumb test: put a drop on your thumb. Pure honey stays put and does not run. Fake honey spreads or drips. The flame test: dip a cotton swab in honey and light it. Pure honey burns because it is flammable. Adulterated honey with water does not light easily. The taste test: pure honey has complex flavoursâfloral, fruity, or woodyâand a slight sting in the throat. Fake honey tastes simply sweet like sugar. The crystallization test: pure honey crystallizes over time (especially if stored cool). Fake honey often stays liquid forever. But note: some pure honey (like acacia) crystallizes slowly. Also, check moisture with a refractometer. Pure honey should be below 20% moisture. Above 20% means it may ferment or be watered down. In Africa, adulteration is common because honey is expensive. A 1-litre bottle of pure honey sells for $8â$15, while sugar syrup costs pennies. As a producer, you can build trust by letting customers test your honey. Sell in clear jars so they can see the colour and texture. Get your honey tested at a local lab or beekeeping association if possible. Always harvest fully capped combs and process cleanly. Your pure honey will speak for itself. Do not be tempted to mix. Short-term gain from adulteration destroys long-term business.

lessons.title: Safety and Hygiene in Honey Handling
lessons.body: Honey is food, so safety and hygiene are non-negotiable. Start with your hands. Wash them with soap and clean water before touching honey or equipment. Wear clean clothes and a hairnet if possible. Do not handle honey if you are sick, especially with diarrhoea or vomiting. Your harvesting toolsâknives, buckets, extractorsâmust be washed and dried. Use food-grade plastic or stainless steel. Never use containers that held chemicals, oil, or fuel. For cleaning, use hot water and a food-safe detergent. Rinse well. Dry with a clean cloth or air dry. During harvest, avoid contaminating honey with dirt, bees, or wax. Use a clean bucket with a lid. Strain honey through a clean cloth or mesh. Do not use your bare hands to squeeze combsâuse a masher or press. After extraction, let honey settle in a tall container. Impurities like wax and bee parts float to the top. Skim them off with a clean spoon. Then pour honey into clean, dry jars. Jars must be sterilized: wash with hot water, then dry in an oven at 100Â°C for 10 minutes, or sun-dry. Do not use wet jarsâmoisture causes fermentation. Seal jars tightly. Store in a cool, dark place, away from strong smells (honey absorbs odours). Never store honey in metal containers because the acid reacts and creates rust. Also, protect yourself from bee stings. Wear your suit and use smoke. If you are allergic, keep an antihistamine nearby. In Africa, many small-scale farmers process honey on the ground or in dirty sheds. This leads to contamination and low prices. Build a simple clean processing area: a table, a roof, and washed walls. Use clean water. Train your family or workers on hygiene. Remember, honey is eaten raw by many people, so any bacteria or dirt can cause illness. Good hygiene means better taste, longer shelf life, and higher prices. Your customers will notice the difference.

quiz.q: What are the two main sugars in honey?
quiz.explanation: Glucose and fructose make up about 80% of honey's weight.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for honey in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Honey with more than 20% moisture can ferment and spoil.

quiz.q: Why should honey not be stored in metal containers?
options: B) Honey's acid reacts with metal, causing rust
quiz.explanation: Honey is acidic and reacts with metal, leading to rust and bad taste.

quiz.q: Which subspecies of Apis mellifera is common in East and Southern Africa?
quiz.explanation: A. m. scutellata is found in East and Southern Africa.

quiz.q: How much honey can a strong Apis mellifera colony produce per year?
quiz.explanation: A strong colony can yield 20â30 kg per year in good conditions.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of stingless bees?
options: B) They are harmless and their honey sells at higher prices
C) They live in large hives
quiz.explanation: Stingless bees do not sting and their honey is valued for medicinal use, fetching higher prices.

quiz.q: Which hive is cheaper and easier to build locally for African farmers?
quiz.explanation: The Kenya Top Bar Hive uses local timber and costs less than the Langstroth.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a bee smoker?
options: B) To calm bees by masking alarm pheromones
quiz.explanation: Smoke calms bees by interfering with their alarm pheromones.

quiz.q: What tool measures honey moisture content?
quiz.explanation: A refractometer measures the moisture level in honey.

quiz.q: When is the best time to harvest honey in East Africa?
options: B) After the rainy season when flowers are abundant
quiz.explanation: Harvest after rains when flowers are plentiful and honey is capped.

quiz.q: What percentage of honey should be left for the colony?
quiz.explanation: Leave at least 30% of honey so the bees do not abscond.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a comb is ready for harvest?
options: A) It is full of bees
B) It is at least 80% capped with white wax
C) It is dark in colour
quiz.explanation: Capped combs indicate the honey is ripe and low in moisture.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for pure honey?
options: A) It dissolves quickly in water
B) It sinks and stays as a lump in water
quiz.explanation: Pure honey is dense and does not dissolve quickly in water.

quiz.q: What does the flame test show?
options: A) Pure honey burns because it is flammable
C) Pure honey does not burn
D) Flame test is not useful
quiz.explanation: Pure honey is flammable; adulterated honey with water does not light easily.

quiz.q: Why does pure honey crystallize?
options: B) It has high glucose content
D) It has too much water
quiz.explanation: Crystallization is natural and depends on the glucose-to-fructose ratio.

quiz.q: What should you do if honey crystallizes?
options: C) Place jar in warm water below 40Â°C
quiz.explanation: Warm water below 40Â°C safely liquefies crystallized honey without destroying enzymes.

quiz.q: Why is hygiene important in honey handling?
options: B) To prevent contamination and illness
quiz.explanation: Honey is eaten raw, so contamination can cause illness and reduce shelf life.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean honey containers?
options: B) Hot water and food-safe detergent
quiz.explanation: Hot water and food-safe detergent effectively clean without leaving harmful residues.

quiz.q: How should jars be prepared before filling with honey?
quiz.explanation: Sterilized, dry jars prevent fermentation and contamination.

quiz.q: What is a sign of adulterated honey?
options: D) It has a slight throat sting
quiz.explanation: Adulterated honey often stays liquid because it lacks natural glucose crystals.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a type of beekeeping equipment?
quiz.explanation: A tractor is not used in beekeeping.

quiz.q: What is the role of a bee brush?
options: B) To gently remove bees from combs
quiz.explanation: A bee brush gently removes bees without harming them.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid harvesting brood combs?
options: B) They contain baby bees and are essential for colony survival
quiz.explanation: Brood combs are where bees raise young; taking them harms the colony.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to harvest honey?
quiz.explanation: Bees are calmer in the evening or early morning, reducing stings.

quiz.q: What does the thumb test for honey involve?
options: A) Putting honey on your thumb to see if it runs
B) Tasting honey on your thumb
C) Smelling honey on your thumb
D) Heating honey on your thumb
quiz.explanation: Pure honey stays put on the thumb; fake honey spreads or drips.

quiz.q: What is a common adulterant in honey?
quiz.explanation: Sugar syrup is commonly added to honey to increase volume and reduce cost.

quiz.q: Why is it important to leave some honey for the bees?
options: B) To prevent absconding and starvation
quiz.explanation: Bees need honey to survive, especially during dry seasons.

quiz.q: What is the first step in honey processing after harvest?
options: B) Straining to remove wax and debris
quiz.explanation: Straining removes impurities before settling and packaging.

quiz.q: Which container is best for storing honey?
options: B) Glass jar or food-grade plastic
quiz.explanation: Glass or food-grade plastic does not react with honey and is easy to clean.

quiz.q: What is a sign of high-quality honey?
options: B) It has a complex flavour and slight throat sting
C) It is very clear and thin
quiz.explanation: Pure honey has complex flavours and a characteristic throat sting.
